title: Oasis Two: the corner, two acts and two envelopes
summary: Their debater takes the floor while they coach from the corner between speeches, the other parent judges and the decision is read for their fingerprints, then acts two and three of the Expedition Talk get their first performance, the family writes the capsule letters, and they run the Sprout's make-ten card.
materials: the sand timers, two minute and one minute, and the call bell
the case file you and your debater have been building since week 5
one grown-up to debate and one to judge, and a blank ballot for the judge
a laptop with an AI assistant, driven by a grown-up who reads its case aloud
the season 2 adder and the season 3 closed ledger, out of their boxes and in your hands
the Expedition dossier, open at the Talk page
two heavy envelopes, paper, and a pen with real ink
the make-ten parent card and a box of blocks, for the teach-someone-younger quest

steps.title: From the corner
steps.body:
For three weeks you have been holding somebody else's case. You took the motion apart with them in week 5 and built the file, and in week 6 you played the nastiest opponent you could invent so that nothing on the floor today would arrive as a surprise.

Today they speak and you do not. That is the whole exercise, and it is harder than debating.

The shape. Your debater takes the floor against the AI, with a grown-up driving it and reading its case aloud. The other grown-up judges, alone, with a ballot. You sit in the corner. You may speak to your debater only between speeches, and only for about as long as one drink of water takes. During a speech you say nothing, signal nothing, and your face does nothing.

One rule about the corner windows, and it is the only coaching rule you get. One thing per window. A coach who hands over four instructions in thirty seconds has handed over none, because a person walking to the front can carry exactly one new idea and no more. Choose which one, and let the other three go.

The corner has a real advantage and today you find out what it is worth. From out there you can see the whole board: what the other side keeps returning to, which of your debater's points nobody has answered, and which one is quietly sinking while everybody talks about something else. The person speaking cannot see any of that, because they are standing inside it.

Then the part that makes this a summit rather than a drill. When the judge reads the decision, you are not listening for who won. You are listening for your fingerprints: which of the things you said in the corner reached a speech, and which of them reached the reasons.

Hand the device to the two grown-ups when you reach the next step.

steps.title: For the debater and the judge only
steps.body:
You two, this step is for you. Hand the device back when you have read it.

Debater: today you are theirs. Argue the case the two of you built, in the order you agreed, and use their signposting even where you would privately have done it differently. If you improvise past the file, say so afterwards, because they need to know which parts of the round were their plan and which were you rescuing yourself. Between speeches, listen to them properly and do what they say, even when you disagree. They have been building the hardest questions they can for a fortnight and they have earned the experiment.

Judge: you judge the round, not the coaching, and you do not soften the ballot because a child helped build the case. Flow it, name the clash, weigh it, decide, and read the decision out loud. Then, and only then, add one extra paragraph out loud that is not part of the decision: where in this round could you see somebody thinking behind the speaker? Name the moments, whether they helped or not, and name at least one that did not.

Whoever drives the AI: type the prompts where they can see the screen, read its case out aloud, and do not clean it up on the way. The old rule holds. The machine is an opponent, not a referee. Nothing it says settles anything, and if it invents a fact or names a study that does not exist, that is the debater's opening rather than a problem the room should tidy away.

And all three of you: they do not speak during a speech. If they start to, wait them out rather than telling them off. The silence is the lesson.

steps.title: The round, and the fingerprints
steps.body:
Run it properly. Constructives two minutes each, rebuttals ninety seconds each, closings one minute each, bell on time, no new arguments in a closing.

Your corner windows sit between speeches and nowhere else. Before each one, look at your own notes and pick the single thing. Then say it in one sentence and stop talking. The stopping is the hard half.

Keep your own sheet through the round, and it is not the judge's sheet. Yours has two columns. One for what the other side keeps coming back to, because whatever they return to is what they think is winning. One for our points that nobody has answered yet, because an unanswered point is free and it is astonishing how often both sides forget it is sitting there.

When the decision is read, listen for your fingerprints rather than the result. Then say out loud which corner note you can hear inside the reasons, and which one you gave that went nowhere at all. Name the one that went nowhere first. That one is the more useful of the two.

Then ask your debater one question and let them answer it without arguing back: which of my corner notes was actually usable while you were standing up, and which one was too big to carry?

Last, one line in your journal that nobody else reads. Was there a moment you wanted to speak during a speech, and what was it about?
checklist: I said nothing during a speech, not with my voice and not with my face
Every corner window gave one thing to do, not a list
I kept my own two-column sheet through the whole round
After the decision I named a corner note that reached the reasons and one that went nowhere
I asked my debater which note was usable on their feet and listened without defending it

steps.title: Acts two and three: the coast and the mountains
steps.body:
The Talk is ten minutes and four acts, one per season, and it gets performed whole in week 12. Act one is drafted. Today you write and perform acts two and three, so that by the finale the only act you have never stood inside is the one about the season you are currently standing inside.

Act two is the coast, which is season 2, and it runs about under three minutes. Hold the adder while you talk. Do not describe it, hold it, and let the room look at it while you speak.

Act three is the mountains, which is season 3, same length, with the closed ledger in your hand.

One instruction for both, and it is the difference between a talk and a list. Each act says what changed, not what happened. What you could not do at the start of that season and could do at the end, one thing that went wrong that you can now tell as a story rather than a wound, and the moment that season ended, whatever you decide that moment was.

The craft note from act one still runs. You planted something in act one that act four has to pay off. Today you either pay a little of it off early, on purpose, so the room feels it coming without knowing why, or you plant a second thing. Whichever you do, write it in the dossier, because week 12 will not remember on its own.

Perform both acts back to back, timed. Then mark one line to cut from each. A first draft of a talk is always long, and choosing what to leave out is a skill of its own.
checklist: Act two is written in the dossier and performed with the adder in my hand
Act three is written in the dossier and performed with the closed ledger in my hand
Each act says what changed in that season, not just what happened in it
I either paid off part of the act one plant or planted a second thing, and wrote down which
I timed both acts back to back and marked one line to cut from each

steps.title: The letters, and two dates in ink
steps.body:
This one happens at the table, with everybody sitting down and the recording off.

Everybody writes a letter, and everybody means everybody: you, both grown-ups, and your Sprout, who will draw theirs or say it out loud for somebody to write down word for word without improving it. Write to whoever you are writing to, later. Nobody reads anybody else's.

Then two envelopes. On the front of each one, in ink, the date it gets opened. Written as a date, the way the wall map does it. Not a number of days, not a number of weeks, not anything that shrinks. A date is a place you are travelling to. A count is a thing standing over your shoulder, and this house does not do those.

Which two dates is a family decision, made out loud tonight rather than assumed. The plan's own suggestion is one envelope for the morning of the first real contest you sit, so that a piece of this summer is in the room on the day, and one for years out, far enough that you will be a different size when it opens. But these are your envelopes and the dates go on them by agreement, not by instruction.

Then seal them and decide out loud where they are going to live, because an envelope nobody can find in three years is a letter that was never written. Say the place, and say who is responsible for it.
checklist: Everybody at the table wrote something, including the youngest, drawn or dictated word for word
Two envelopes, each with its opening date written on the front in ink
The dates are written as dates, with no count of days or weeks anywhere on them
The family agreed out loud where the envelopes will live and who is responsible for them
Both envelopes are sealed and nobody read anybody else's letter

steps.title: Teach someone younger
steps.body:
They watched you sit in a corner all morning and say nothing. Now you get a chair of your own beside them.

Today you run their make-ten card, the tower game, the one where you build a tower and they build the partner tower that finishes the ten. Read the card all the way through before you start, so you know where it lands.

The idea underneath it is small and worth saying in their words rather than yours: if you know the whole and you know one part, the other part is hiding in your hands. Say that once, with your hands, and then stop explaining.

Build your tower first and let them build the partner. When they get it wrong, do not tell them. Count with them, out loud, from their tower up to ten, and let the counting be the correction. That is the whole coaching move, and it is the same one you spent this morning learning: one thing per window, and then quiet.

Somewhere in the middle, try the one that goes past building: say a number and see whether they can name its partner without stacking anything. If they can, that is worth noticing. If they cannot, that is also worth noticing, and you go back to the blocks with no fuss and no face.

Finish with the question, and then wait: which pair was the easiest? Let them answer in their own words, however they say it, and do not tidy it up.
checklist: I read the card all the way through before I started
I built one tower and let them build the partner tower themselves
When they were wrong I counted up to ten with them instead of telling them
I tried at least one pair without blocks and noticed what happened either way
I asked which pair was easiest and waited for their own words

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt:
Record two things. First, the judge reading the decision, and then you, straight afterwards, saying out loud which of your corner notes you can hear inside it and which one went nowhere. Second, acts two and three performed back to back with the adder and the ledger in your hands.

Then keep rolling for one honest sentence: what did you see from the corner that you would never have seen from the floor?
